Polynomial Degree 3

AlgebraComplex AnalysisCurves
Game: Shape a curve with four sliders and see where it crosses the line in the middle.
How to play: Move the sliders. Green dots show where the curve hits zero; click the small dark dot in the middle of the bend to see a straight line touch it there.

Look for the math

A third degree equation ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 with a ≠ 0 has three roots. At least one is always real; the other two are either both real (perhaps equal) or a pair of complex numbers re ± im·i. The applet draws that pair as two points straight above and below each other, at height ±im.

Why one root is always real

For large x the term ax³ wins, so P(x) has one sign far to the right and the opposite sign far to the left. A continuous curve that goes from below the axis to above it must cross it: that is Bolzano's theorem. The applet uses exactly this idea to find the root: from x = 0 it steps by 1 towards the sign change, then halves the bracket until |P(x)| < 0.001 (the bisection method). Dividing by x − r with Horner's method leaves a quadratic for the other two. The test compared this search with the applet's code on 5,832 cubics and checked every set of three roots against the coefficients.

The inflection point

The curve bends one way on one side of x₀ = −b/(3a) and the other way on the other side. It is symmetric about that inflection point: P(x₀ + h) + P(x₀ − h) = 2P(x₀), so turning the picture half a turn about it gives the same curve. Take away the tangent line there and what is left is a(x − x₀)³, a cubic with three equal roots, shown in red when the tangent is on. The test checked both on 20,000 random cubics.

Make b = 0, c = 0 and slide d: the curve moves up and down, and the two complex roots slide along their dashed line. What does c do to the number of real roots?
